thesis: Nuh's declared tawakkul is what empties his people's threats of power, frees his call from any wage-claim on them, and the closing history (denial, rescue, succession, drowning) proves that denial does not own the outcome.
notes: Clean. Every interpretive move lands on a classical anchor. al-Tabari's own summary of 17:71 is the file's thesis verbatim in substance ('إنه بنصرة الله له عليهم واثق، ومن كيدهم وبوائقهم غير خائف'), and he adds that the story is a حث to the Prophet to imitate Nuh — which is exactly the file's framing. Checks that verified: (1) maqami = 'my staying among you and its being burdensome' (al-Tabari: 'عظم عليكم مقامي بين أظهركم وشقّ عليكم'; Jalalayn: 'لبثي فيكم'); (2) shuraka' = their idols/deities (al-Tabari: 'وعني بالشركاء آلهتهم وأوثانهم'; Ibn Kathir: 'get together with all of your deities'); (3) ghummah = obscurity/confusion, i.e. 'make it plain, decide openly' — the file's reading is al-Tabari ('ملتبسًا مشكلا مبهمًا', with the هلال/غُمّ shahid), al-Jalalayn ('مستورًا بل أظهروه وجاهروني به') and al-Muyassar ('لا تجعلوا أمركم عليكم مستترًا بل ظاهرًا منكشفًا') in agreement; (4) iqdu ilayya wa la tunziruni = carry it out, no delay (Qatadah, Mujahid); (5) khala'if = the saved remnant made successors in the land over the deniers (al-Tabari: 'وجعلنا الذين نجينا مع نوح في السفينة خلائف في الأرض من قومه الذين كذبوه'); (6) the wage/fear pairing — Ibn Kathir himself supplies the Hud parallel (11:54-55) the file's Theme 2 relies on. No countable or superlative claims anywhere in the file, so nothing needed corpus adjudication. Not ahkam-bearing, not contested. No truncated tafsir blocks (the file paraphrases rather than quoting tafsir at length). Only housekeeping note for the human: frontmatter still reads validated: false.

thesis: The awliya' of Allah are not a mystical elite but exactly those whom the next ayah defines — those who believed and kept practicing taqwa — and their freedom from fear and grief is guaranteed by unalterable divine speech.
notes: Strongest of the three. The thesis is al-Tabari's own tarjih word for word: 'والصواب من القول في ذلك أن يقال: الولي — أعني ولي الله — هو من كان بالصفة التي وصفه الله بها، وهو الذي آمن واتقى'. Every named attribution was checked against the fetched text and all match: (1) al-Tabari glosses awliya' as ansar and wali as nasir ('والأولياء جمع ولي، وهو النصير') — file says exactly this; (2) al-Tabari's 'no fear in the Hereafter from Allah's punishment because He is pleased with them, no grief over what of dunya passed them by' — matches the file's Theme 2 paragraph including the reason-clause the file attributes to him; (3) the reported view 'people whose appearance brings Allah to mind' is present ('هم قومٌ يُذْكَرُ الله لرؤيتهم') and the file correctly labels it as one reported view among a stated ikhtilaf ('واختلف أهل التأويل فيمن يستحق هذا الاسم'); (4) Ibn Kathir's 'every pious, God-fearing person is a friend of Allah' — verbatim in the fetched English; (5) the grammar section is precise — al-Tabari does say alladhina amanu is 'من نعت الأولياء', does raise the raf'/nasb question ('أفي موضع رفع أم في موضع نصب؟'), and does answer raf' ('قيل: في موضع رفع'); (6) al-Tabari's working definition of taqwa 'بأداء فرائضه واجتناب معاصيه' and al-Muyassar's iman gloss both match; (7) al-Muyassar on la tabdil ('لا يخلف الله وعده ولا يغيره') and on al-fawz al-'azim ('اشتمل على النجاة من كل محذور، والظفر بكل مطلوب محبوب') match the file's paraphrases exactly. On the point raised in the assignment — the 'glad tidings = righteous dream' reading: the file handles it correctly and does NOT need a hadith citation, because it never asserts it as a hadith. It attributes it as a reported tafsir position inside an ikhtilaf the file explicitly names ('Al-Tabari states plainly that the early scholars differed over what this worldly bushra is'), calls it 'the best-known reported position', and closes with 'the tradition preserved more than one answer rather than settling on one.' That framing is accurate to al-Tabari, who opens with 'ثم اختلف أهل التأويل في البشرى... فقال بعضهم: هي الرؤيا الصالحة يراها الرجل المسلم أو ترى له، وفي الآخرة الجنة' and then runs the Abu al-Darda'/'Ubada b. al-Samit turuq. If a citation is ever wanted, the fetched sources supply one for free: al-Jalalayn grades it — 'فسرت في حديث صححه الحاكم بالرؤيا الصالحة يراها الرجل أو ترى له' — and Ibn Kathir routes it through Ibn Jarir from 'Ubada. Optional enrichment, not a defect. One small imprecision worth zero action: the file contrasts al-Muyassar as keeping the bushra 'broad' against the dream-reading, but al-Muyassar actually does both ('بما يسرهم، ومنها الرؤيا الصالحة') — he lists the dream as one instance of the broad category, which if anything strengthens the file's point. No countable claims in the file; the grammatical claims (indefinite khawf, kana + imperfect, definite al-bushra, fronted lahum, huwa as pronoun of separation) all verify against the Uthmani text and corpus segments. Frontmatter still reads validated: false.

thesis: The Isra' opening teaches that the highest divine honors are meant to deepen servanthood and gratitude rather than entitlement, and that when a carried people forget this, consequence returns on them as a moral law of history.

flags.quote: Then the passage moves into one of the starkest historical warnings in the Quran:
flags.issue: Rubric check 4 (adab on contested passages). The file gives 17:4-8 a full linguistic section and a full theme, but nowhere acknowledges the ikhtilaf that the classical sources foreground on precisely this passage. Ibn Kathir, in the fetched text, stops to say so explicitly: 'The earlier and later commentators differed over the identity of these invaders. Many Isra'iliyyat (reports from Jewish sources) were narrated about this, but I did not want to make this book too long by mentioning them, because some of them are fabricated...' al-Tabari carries several incompatible identifications (Ibn 'Abbas: three Persian kings; Qatadah: the episode ending with 'this tribe of the Arabs'; Sa'id b. al-Musayyib via Ibn Kathir: Nebuchadnezzar). This is the single most adversarially-quoted passage in the file's range, and it currently reads as a settled historical account with no methodological framing. Note this is a gap, not an error: the file names no invader, no date, and no modern people, and imports zero isra'iliyyat — which is why the severity is moderate and the fix is additive.

flags.quote: And Bani Isra'il are reminded that they too come from people who were carried by Allah, yet the standard held before them is Nuh as `abdan shakura`.
flags.issue: Narrower than al-Tabari's own preferred reading, and narrower than the file's own moral. al-Tabari takes dhurriyyata man hamalna ma'a Nuh to address all humankind, not Bani Isra'il specifically: 'وعنى بالذرية: جميع من احتجّ عليه جلّ ثناؤه بهذا القرآن من أجناس الأمم، عربهم وعجمهم من بني إسرائيل وغيرهم، وذلك أنّ كلّ من على الأرض من بني آدم، فهم من ذرية من حمله الله مع نوح في السفينة' (Mujahid likewise: 'من بني إسرائيل وغيرهم'; Qatadah: 'والناس كلهم ذرّية من أنجى الله في تلك السفينة'). Not false — Bani Isra'il are inside the address — but the file spends Theme 2 arguing the warning is everyone's mirror, and al-Tabari hands it that universality directly at 17:3. Reads as a missed anchor rather than a misattribution.

flags.quote: The Prophet's Night Journey is the most staggering earthly honor given to a human being before the Hereafter, yet the ayah identifies him through servanthood.
flags.issue: A superlative asserted flatly and not mechanically verifiable. No classical source in the fetch ranks the Isra' this way; the closest is Ibn Kathir's 'This indicates that he is the greatest leader of all,' which is about the Prophet's rank among the prophets, not a ranking of honors. Devotionally uncontroversial and nothing in the file depends on it, but by rubric check 2 an unverifiable absolute gets recorded. Softening to 'one of the most staggering' costs nothing.

notes: The thesis itself is solidly grounded — al-Muyassar states the file's exact moral as his own closing comment on 17:8: 'وفي هذه الآية وما قبلها، تحذير لهذه الأمة من العمل بالمعاصي؛ لئلا يصيبها مثل ما أصاب بني إسرائيل، فسنن الله واحدة لا تبدَّل ولا تغيَّر.' Ibn Kathir grounds the gratitude half at 17:3 ('follow in the footsteps of your father... he was a grateful servant'), al-Jalalayn grounds shakur as 'كثير الشكر لنا حامدًا في جميع أحواله', and 'asa rabbukum an yarhamakum as an open door conditioned on repentance is exactly al-Muyassar ('أن يرحمكم بعد انتقامه إن تبتم وأصلحتم') and al-Jalalayn ('بعد المرة الثانية إن تبتم') — so the file's 'Mercy is still possible. Return is still possible' is grounded, not sentimental. Specifically on the two risks named in the assignment, both come back clean: (a) NO isra'iliyyat — the file identifies no invader, no king, no empire, no date, and no modern people, which is the harder discipline than Ibn Kathir himself required; (b) NO over-claim on the Aqsa or the mi'raj — the file renders al-Masjid al-Aqsa only as 'the Farthest Mosque', never asserts a location or an identification, and never mentions the ascension, Buraq, the prophets' prayer, or the fifty-prayers episode at all, though Ibn Kathir's entry carries all of it. If anything it under-uses what it is entitled to. Corpus verification run: 'abd (root عبد) does occur at 17:1, 17:3 and 17:5; asra is root سري while hamalna is root حمل, so the 'carried' motif spans two different verbs — the file is honest about this ('That repeated motif of being carried is not accidental in effect, even if the settings differ') and the real lexical link it leans on, 'abdihi at 17:1 against 'abdan shakura at 17:3, is genuine; 'uluww (root علو) appears twice in 17:4 and once in 17:7; 'udtum/'udna are both root عود in 17:8. No count-claims are made, so no normalization issue arose. One translation choice the reviewer may want to know about but which needs no change: the file renders hasir at 17:8 as 'a prison', which follows Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn Kathir, al-Muyassar and al-Jalalayn — but al-Tabari's own tarjih is the minority reading 'فراشا ومهادا' (a spread bedding). The file builds nothing on the word, so this is informational only. Recommended fix, one paragraph, before Theme 2 or at the head of the 17:4-8 section: state that the commentators differed over which two historical episodes are meant and who the 'servants of severe might' were, that Ibn Kathir deliberately declined to relay the isra'iliyyat about them, and that the passage is read here as a sunnah of Allah addressed to every community that mistakes rescue for immunity — not as a verdict on any present-day people. That one addition clears this flag and makes the file's existing restraint explicit instead of merely implicit. Frontmatter still reads validated: false.
